title: World Games
build: Epyx disk, 1986, two sides (C64 Preservation Project G64s, world_games_s1[epyx_1986](pal) and world_games_s2[epyx_1986](pal), MD5 2ab5a751... and f983b43d...)

records.c: the title part's entry, from the shell's $0991. Stops CIA 1's and CIA 2's timers and turns their interrupts off, sets up the bitmap screen ($12CC), makes the globe's map in three more positions ($1354), builds the music's frequency table ($186E), copies the picture's screen colours ($7F40) to $4000 and its colour RAM ($8328) to $D800, sets the globe's sprites ($12FE), starts the raster interrupt at line 250 ($10D1), colours the credits ($1290), draws the globe ($1146) and starts the title tune
the unpacker's read of the header's second byte (the pair table's high byte); here, inside the title's code
the unpacker's read of the header's third byte (the packed data's low byte); here, inside the title's code
the unpacker's read of the header's fourth byte (the packed data's high byte); here, inside the title's code

the shell's unpacker reads the packed file's header here ($1000-$1004 and $10FF, through its own indexes) while it unpacks; once it is done, the title's code is here, its start-up going on with the CIA timers
waits for the fire button on either joystick, or for the tune to end (voice 1's data pointer cleared, $A1) and then about a third of a second more

the title is over: at raster line 0, interrupts off, the interrupt's "screen on" changed into LDA #$00 ($1136) so it cannot switch the screen back on, the screen blanked, the sound silenced, then the shell's restart at $0900, which loads the menu

the raster interrupt at the top of the screen (line 0; line 250 the first time). Every 385 frames (55 times seven, counted by $1E) it swaps the credits shown at the bottom ($1F, $1290). It shows the bitmap at $6000 ($D018 = $09), plays the music ($18B7) and sets the next interrupt at line 218 ($1268). Every seventh frame ($11) it turns the globe a step ($1151), turns its sprites on and the screen on
the shell's unpacker reads the packed file's last header offset here before the title's own bytes replace it; here, the middle of the interrupt routine
ORA #$10 sets the screen-on bit; $10B9 rewrites it as LDA #$00 at the end
the operand of the ORA that turns the screen on, which $10BE replaces with 0
draws the globe at the start: its map from $6BC0 down, with no step first ($1165)

turns the globe one step: the next of four positions within a character cell ($1B, 0-3), and after four, the next cell of the map ($10, counting down from 10 and wrapping from 1 to 20); falls into the drawing

draws the globe into the bitmap: six rows of nine cells (72 bytes) from cell 16 of row 9 ($6BC0), each the map strip of the position in $1B ($1497) from cell $10, ANDed with that row's circle mask ($125C): the loop's three operands are rewritten for each row. The first time ($1A) it also sets the globe's colours: $15 in the screen ($4178) and 6 in colour RAM ($D978)
the copy of one row: map AND mask into the bitmap, 72 bytes; the three $FFFF operands are filled in above
the low byte of the map read's operand
the operand of the map read: its low byte at $11D2, its high byte here, written for each row
the low byte of the mask read's operand
the operand of the mask read, written for each row
the low byte of the bitmap write's operand
the operand of the bitmap write, written for each row
the circle mask of each of the globe's six rows, bottom row first (read with the row count, 6 down to 1): 72 bytes each, from $3960 to $3B0F
the high bytes of the mask list
the raster interrupt at line 218, above the credits: the bitmap for the bottom of the screen, $6000 or $4000 by $1F, so the credits there change; then back to $10D1 at line 0

colours the credits' rows in the screen at $4000 and in colour RAM: yellow ($77) and light blue ($EE) for the credits in the picture at $6000, cyan ($33) and a few cells yellow for the other set, in the picture at $4000
sprites off, the screen blanked, VIC bank 1 ($4000-$7FFF), multicolour bitmap mode with the screen at $4000 and the bitmap at $6000, border and background black
six multicolour sprites behind the bitmap, two rows of three, at the globe: shapes $60-$65 ($5800-$597F), colour 11 with the shared colours 12 and 1, positions from $1344
the six sprites' positions, X then Y, then four zeros for sprites 6 and 7

makes three more copies of the globe's map, each one multicolour pixel (two bits) further to the right than the one before, with the pixel that falls off the right end coming back at the left: $3000 to $A000, $A000 to $A780, $A780 to $AF00. Each copy is six strips of 40 cells (320 bytes), from the lists at $145B and $1491
one pixel row of a strip: 40 cells, each byte shifted right two bits, taking in the bits the last cell shifted out
the three lists of six strips each, as sources: $3000-$3640, $A000-$A640, $A780-$ADC0; $145B points to them
the third source list, the strips of the second copy
the source list being worked on, copied here from the list $145B names
the source list's high bytes
where the three source lists start ($142B, $1437, $1443)
the source lists' starting addresses' high bytes
the destination list being worked on, copied here from the list $1491 names
the destination list's high bytes
the three lists of six strips each, as destinations: $A000-$A640, $A780-$ADC0, $AF00-$B540
where the three destination lists start ($146D, $1479, $1485)
the destination lists' starting addresses' high bytes
the map strip for each of the globe's four positions within a cell: $3000 as authored, then the copies at $A000, $A780 and $AF00
the high bytes of the globe's four map strips

the title tune's first voice: notes and commands for the music driver at $18B7. A byte below $C0 is a note, two times its number indexing the frequency table, $60 a rest, followed by its length in frames, bit 7 set to hold the gate into the next note; $C0-$E0 are commands with their own arguments ($1C76), $FF ends the voice
the title tune's second voice
the title tune's third voice
the shell's unpacker's copy loop has $1800 as a placeholder operand; here, the title's music data
the track each voice plays in the title's one tune: 0, 1 and 2 for voices 1, 2 and 3. A tune's entry starts at four times its number, less two, so the fourth byte, $FF, is not read
where each track starts: $149F, $1630, $1770
the track pointers' high bytes

starts tune A: for each voice, the track the tune gives it ($1836), its data pointer ($A0-$A5) and a wait of one frame ($C1-$C3); a voice whose entry is $FF is left as it is. The processor's interrupt flag is kept
builds the music's frequency table at $C000: eight octaves of twelve notes, 192 bytes, each octave the top one ($1CB8) shifted right, note n at $C000 + 2n; then silences the SID ($18A6)
silences the music: clears the SID's registers ($D401 on) and the driver's variables ($A0-$DF), and sets the pulse sweep's start to $0400

plays one frame of music, from the raster interrupt. For each voice, 3 down to 1: when the note's frames run out the gate is let go, unless held, and the next commands and note are read ($18E1); then the pulse width sweep for the voices that have it ($CC), up and down between $0200 and $0E00 by $0F a frame, or $10 when the carry is left set (nothing clears it before the addition), and the vibrato for those that have it ($D2), each voice's frequency moved up or down by its step and turned round after its period
reads the voice's next byte: $EA is skipped, $FF ends the voice (pointer cleared, gate off), below $C0 a note ($1C08), otherwise a command from the table at $1C76
the next voice
the pulse width, the same for every voice that sweeps

the vibrato: every voice in $D2 counts its period down ($D9) and turns its direction round (bit 7 of $D4) when it runs out, adding or subtracting the step to its frequency; then the three frequencies are written to the SID
the offset of each voice's registers from $D400: 0, 7 and 14
command $C1: the voice's frequency, two bytes, straight to the SID
command $DD: a pulse wave ($40) with the pulse width at $0800
command $C2: the voice's waveform (its control register without the gate), one byte
command $C3: the voice's pulse width, two bytes
command $C4: the voice's envelope, attack-decay then sustain-release
command $C5: the filter's cutoff, low then high byte
command $C9: lowers the filter's cutoff by a byte, then reads a length as a note does
command $D6: raises the filter's cutoff by a byte, then a length
command $C6: the filter's resonance, the high nibble of a byte
command $C0: adds a byte to the volume, the result kept below 16
command $C7: the volume, the low nibble of a byte, with the filter type kept
command $C8: a wait: the voice reads nothing more for that many frames
command $CA: puts the voice through the filter
command $CB: the filter type, the high nibble of a byte, with the volume kept
command $CC: takes the voice out of the filter
command $CD: sets the voice's first repeat count ($B7)
command $CE: a repeat: two bytes, an address the voice goes back to until the first repeat count runs out
command $D1: sets the voice's second repeat count ($B4)
command $D2: the second repeat, as $CE with the count at $B4
command $DA: lowers the frequency's high byte by a byte, then a length
command $CF: lowers the frequency by a byte, then a length
command $D9: raises the frequency's high byte by a byte, then a length
command $D0: raises the frequency by a byte, then a length
command $DB: vibrato on for the voice: its step and direction ($D4), then its period ($D3, $D9)
command $DC: vibrato off for the voice
command $D3: pulse width sweep on for the voice
command $D4: pulse width sweep off for the voice
each voice's bit, 1, 2 and 4, for the driver's masks of voices
each voice's bit cleared, $FE, $FD and $FB
command $D7: detune on for the voice: a byte the note's frequency is lowered by
command $D8: detune off
command $D5: a random note, number 31 to 95, which the SID's voice 3 output ($D41B) picks

command $DE: sets $DC to $FF, lets the gate go, and ends the voice's reading for the frame. The waveform it reads is at $AE plus twice the voice's number, X still holding the data pointer's index: the right one for voice 1 only
command $DF: sets the voice's bit in $DD and stores a byte in $DE
command $E0: clears the voice's bit in $DD

a note: two times its number indexes the frequency table at $C000; the rest note, $60, only lets the gate go. The frequency goes to the SID, lowered by the voice's detune if it has it; the gate on. Then its length ($1C50)
the note's length: bit 7 holds the gate when the length runs out, bits 0-6 are the frames
the next byte of the voice's data, through its pointer at $A0 + $BF, which steps on
where each command, $C0 to $E0, is handled
the command handlers' high bytes
the twelve notes of the top octave, C to B, as SID frequencies ($861E to $FD2E); $186E shifts them for the seven octaves below
the top octave's high bytes
where each octave starts in the frequency table at $C000, by the number of shifts plus one: the first byte is not read

the globe's map of the world: a strip six character rows high and 40 cells round (6 x 320 bytes, $3000-$377F), multicolour bitmap cells with the land and the sea; $1354 makes three copies of it moved on by one, two and three pixels, and the globe shows a 9-cell window of it, which moves round; $3000-$33FF
the rest of the world map, $3400-$377F
the globe's round outline as bitmap masks, six rows of 72 bytes (nine cells), $3960-$3B0F, the top row first in memory: ANDed with the map so that only the disc of the globe is drawn
the six sprites behind the globe ($12FE), shapes $60-$65 of VIC bank 1, 64 bytes each
the other set of credits, the bottom four character rows (rows 21-24) of a second bitmap whose rows start at $4000; the interrupt at line 218 shows it every other 385 frames; $5A40-$5E3F
the rest of the other credits' rows, $5E40-$5F3F

the title picture, a multicolour bitmap of 8000 bytes at $6000-$7F3F, with its screen colours at $7F40 and its colour RAM at $8328: the Epyx logo, WORLD GAMES and the credits at the bottom; the globe's window (rows 9-14, cells 16-24) is redrawn by $1165. $6000-$63FF

the title picture's bitmap, $7C00-$7F3F
the title picture's screen colours, 1000 bytes, copied to $4000 by the start-up ($102B, four pages, so 24 bytes of the colour RAM data after it go to $43E8 too); $7F40-$803F
the screen colours go on across $8000: $8000-$803F
the screen colours, $8040-$813F
the screen colours, $8140-$823F
the screen colours, $8240-$8327, and the start of the colour RAM data
the title picture's colour RAM, 1000 bytes, copied to $D800 by the start-up (four pages, to $8727); $8328-$8427
